name: Framework
description: A typed API and frontend client from your Prisma schema.
headline: Your schema. Every layer connected.
detail: Keep your Prisma schema, client and migrations. Aventara turns your models and configuration into contracts, a typed HTTP API and a frontend client.

pitch.storyTitle: Stop describing the same data. Again.
pitch.storyBody: Your database schema already describes your data. Aventara carries that shape through the API and into your frontend, so you can spend your time on what your application actually does.

capabilities.title: One model. A deliberate API.
capabilities.body: Compile your Prisma schema and configuration into contracts that describe resources, fields and operations. Choose what your API exposes.

capabilities.title: A different view for every layer.
capabilities.body: Hide sensitive fields, make them write-only, or turn off frontend operations while server code keeps full access.

capabilities.title: Types that follow your query.
capabilities.body: Select the fields you need. Your generated client knows the result shape, with no runtime dependency on Aventara packages.

capabilities.title: Your business logic belongs here.
capabilities.body: Add guards, pipes and hooks through pipelines. Compose transactions with typed references between steps.

workflow.title: Every layer, connected.
workflow.body: Your schema and configuration become a contract. NestJS or Next.js serves it. Your frontend gets a typed client generated from the deployed contract.

scenarios.label: User
scenarios.caption: The selected fields shape your result. Your Prisma schema stays the source.

scenarios.label: Post
scenarios.caption: Filter through a typed client. Keep the query close to the UI that needs it.

pitch.ctaTitle: Your next API starts with a schema.
pitch.ctaBody: Create a project, connect your models, and build the parts that make your application yours.

faq.question: Do I keep my Prisma client and migrations?
faq.answer: Yes. Your application owns its Prisma client, schema and migrations. Aventara extends your ORM and runs operations through the adapter.

faq.question: Which hosts can serve the API?
faq.answer: NestJS 12 on Express or Fastify, or a Next.js App Router app on the supported Node runtime. The docs cover both hosts.

faq.question: Do I need Access?
faq.answer: Access is optional. The framework works on its own; Access adds schema-typed authorization when your application needs it.

faq.question: Is the API stable?
faq.answer: The framework is a release candidate. Breaking changes are still possible before a stable release. Pin versions and follow the upgrade guide.

name: Access
description: Authorization, typed from your schema. Every row. Every field.
headline: Know exactly who can do what.
detail: Write role-first rules that follow your schema. Access decides which rows and fields a caller may use. Better Auth handles sign-in and credentials.
features: Audit the rule behind a decision

pitch.storyTitle: Who can do what should be easy to answer.
pitch.storyBody: As your application grows, permission checks spread across handlers and services. Access gives those decisions a home: role-first rules, typed from your schema, with an explanation behind each decision.

capabilities.title: A typo should fail before a request.
capabilities.body: Resource names, fields, relations and enum values are checked against your schema. Mistakes surface at the key that names them.

capabilities.title: Permission is explicit.
capabilities.body: Nothing is allowed until a grant allows it. Any matching deny wins, regardless of rule order. Missing values fail closed.

capabilities.title: One engine. Every kind of caller.
capabilities.body: Apply decisions to sessions, bearer tokens, MCP agents and server code. Agents are held to their user’s grants and token scopes.

capabilities.title: See the rule behind the answer.
capabilities.body: Record authorization decisions in the audit log. Trace the rule that decided, so permission changes have a reason you can inspect.

workflow.title: Identity in. A decision out.
workflow.body: Better Auth handles sign-in and credentials. Access resolves permissions. The framework validates and runs the operation. Each part has a clear job.

steps.title: Identify the caller
steps.body: A session or bearer token supplies the principal for the request.

steps.title: Resolve the rules
steps.body: Access evaluates grants and denies for the resource, action, rows and fields.

steps.title: Enforce the decision
steps.body: The framework applies the decision. Refused requests return 403 A4002.

demo.label: A RULE. A CALLER. A DECISION.

scenarios.label: Author
scenarios.output:
Caller    Ada · id user_ada
Action    update Note
Row       authorId: "user_ada"
Banned    false
scenarios.caption: The author can edit their own note. This is a local illustration of the quickstart rules.

scenarios.label: Other user
scenarios.output:
Caller    Grace · id user_grace
Action    update Note
Row       authorId: "user_ada"
Banned    false
scenarios.caption: Being signed in is not enough to edit someone else’s note. No matching grant means no permission.

scenarios.label: Banned author
scenarios.output:
Caller    Ada · id user_ada
Action    update Note
Row       authorId: "user_ada"
Banned    true
scenarios.caption: The author’s grant still matches. The banned-user deny takes precedence.

pitch.ctaBody: Start with the Note example. Write your first rules, allow a request, and see another refused.

faq.question: Does Access sign users in?
faq.answer: Better Auth handles sign-in and issues credentials. Access adds authorization: which rows and fields a caller may use.

faq.question: Can I use the authentication I already have?
faq.answer: Yes. Use the policy engine alone with your own authentication, add the Access plugin to your existing Better Auth setup, or set both up together with createAccess.

faq.question: What happens when a grant and a deny both match?
faq.answer: The deny wins. Rule order does not change the result. A request with no matching grant is denied too.

faq.question: Can several services share policies?
faq.answer: Each service can own a namespace in the Access registry. The CLI can push, pull and verify policy files; a generated client supports services that do not run on Aventara.
